findings.exact_estimate: Qualitative descriptive findings (n = 18 interviews, no statistical test; PDF pp. 18-19): ₱6,000 utility connection fee + ₱4,000 to ₱8,000 pipe installation cost = ₱10,000 to ₱14,000 ($234 to $327) total upfront cost (vs. ₱15,174 mean monthly income); typical installment plan requires ₱3,000 initial payment + ₱3,000 over 3 months, whereas low-income unconnected interviewees reported affording at most ₱300 to ₱500 ($7 to $12) per month.
findings.exposure_and_reference: Upfront BWD utility connection fees, piping costs, case-by-case installment plan terms, and application processing / informal payment barriers (qualitative analysis)
findings.finding_label: Utility connection fees, installment terms, and administrative/informal barriers -> Household ability to obtain BWD connection (qualitative)
findings.outcome_and_polarity: Ability of low-income households to obtain a formal household BWD metered water connection (barriers exclude low-income households and force reliance on costlier delivery trucks [4x BWD price], purified jugs [11x BWD price], or neighbor resale)

headline_result_summary: In a mixed-methods study of 396 randomly sampled households (and 18 in-depth interviews) in Pinget, Baguio City, Philippines, the headline institutional/infrastructure finding is that having an own-household metered connection to the quasi-governmental municipal water utility (Baguio Water District, BWD)—relative to no BWD connection—is positively and significantly associated with all four household water security outcomes: +27.2% higher water consumption (Est. = 0.24, SE = 0.07, p < .01), higher perceived cleanliness (Est. = 0.35, SE = 0.13, p < .01), higher odds of extreme ease of access (OR = 2.16, p < .01), and higher odds of affordable water expenses <=10% of income (OR = 2.76, p < .05). However, shared/other BWD connections show mixed associations (higher affordability OR = 2.71, p < .05, but 20.8% lower consumption Est. = −0.23, p < .001, and null cleanliness and ease), homeownership (tenure) has statistically null associations across all four outcomes, and qualitative interviews identify high upfront connection costs (₱6,000 fee plus ₱4,000–₱8,000 piping = ₱10,000–₱14,000), restrictive case-by-case installment plans, slow bureaucracy, and informal "under the table" payment practices as barriers excluding low-income households from connecting.
specification_or_coding_pitfalls: 1. Exposure-selection divergence across review families: Depending on which review construct S882 was mapped to, the direction differs sharply: (a) Own-household municipal utility connection (BWD vs. none) is uniformly positive/favorable across all 4 outcomes; (b) Shared/other BWD connection vs. none is mixed (+affordability OR = 2.71, −consumption Est. = −0.23, null cleanliness and ease); (c) Homeownership (property tenure, 1 = yes vs. 0 = no) is completely null across all 4 outcomes (Est. = 0.09, 0.20, −0.07 [OR 0.94], −0.26 [OR 0.77], all p >= .05); and (d) Upfront utility connection fees (₱10,000–₱14,000 combined cost), restrictive installment plans, and informal "under the table" application barriers are qualitative findings showing exclusionary/unfavorable barriers to access (not estimated as regression variables). 2. Affordability polarity trap: Affordability is coded 1 = water expenses <= 10.0% of household income and 0 = > 10.0% of income, so positive coefficients / OR > 1 indicate BETTER affordability (lower expenditure share), whereas negative coefficients (e.g., logged tank/drum capacity Est. = −0.61, OR = 0.54, p < .05) indicate WORSE affordability (higher cost burden). 3. Social network reverse-causality/question-wording artifact: Money-borrowing network of 2+ HHs vs. 0 HHs has a negative association with perceived ease (Est. = −0.91, OR = 0.40, p < .05; authors report inverse OR = 2.49 for 0 HHs vs. 2+ HHs), which the author notes reflects water-secure households answering "zero" because they never needed to borrow.
study_design: Mixed-methods cross-sectional study: stratified random household survey analyzed via multiple linear and logistic regression with multiple imputation (10 datasets), compound-level clustering, and finite population correction, paired with purposive in-depth qualitative interviews
unit_and_sample_size: Households (self-identified household water managers) in Pinget neighborhood, Baguio City: N = 396 surveyed households (from 416 eligible sampled out of 1,793 housing units; 95.2% participation rate) and n = 18 purposively sampled qualitative interview participants
